title: Paroxysmal Network State and the Network Polarity Principle: A Multiscale Neuroimmune Framework for Inflammatory Neuropsychiatric Disorders
content: The sickness behavior model explains many neuropsychiatric consequences of peripheral inflammation, including fatigue, anhedonia, and depressed mood, but does not account for the marked heterogeneity of presentations across inflammatory disorders, particularly paradoxical positive-polarity manifestations such as euphoria and behavioral disinhibition. We propose the Paroxysmal Network State (PNS), a transient, metastable reconfiguration of large-scale brain networks emerging during inflammatory disease activity through convergent neuroimmune pathways (humoral, vagal, and microglia-mediated signaling), together with the Network Polarity Principle (NPP), which holds that clinical phenotype emerges from the interaction between inflammatory perturbation and the functional identity of the reorganizing neural networks, rather than from inflammatory burden alone. Candidate determinants of individual variability include baseline network architecture, cerebellar circuitry, brain reserve, neuromodulatory and hormonal state, prior inflammatory history, and immunogenetic background. Experimental cerebellar inflammation models demonstrate that inflammatory signaling can induce reversible network reorganization via microglia-mediated changes in intrinsic neuronal excitability. Transdiagnostic neuroimaging evidence across depression, psychosis, rheumatoid arthritis, and multiple sclerosis, together with domain-dissociated behavioral findings in human cerebellar ataxia, provides convergent biological plausibility. We ground the model’s attractor-based account in a levels-of-explanation (supervenience) argument linking network- and clinical-level descriptions, and identify a candidate sustained, non-remitting patient subgroup as an explicit boundary condition. We outline falsifiable predictions spanning longitudinal network dynamics, neurophysiological biomarkers, topographic determination of clinical polarity, and treatment-related reversibility. Rather than replacing existing neuroimmune models, PNS–NPP offers a systems-level hypothesis linking neuroimmune mechanisms to transient network states and network-dependent clinical heterogeneity, generating explicit predictions for experimental testing.
